title: Batteries, fuel cells and corrosion
competency: Describe primary and secondary batteries and fuel cells, explain corrosion as an electrochemical process and how to prevent it.

keywords.def: A battery used once and thrown away, such as a dry cell.
A rechargeable battery, such as a lead–acid car battery.
A cell that runs on a continuous supply of fuel (H₂) and oxygen.
The slow destruction of a metal by an electrochemical reaction with its surroundings.
Coating iron with zinc, which corrodes instead of the iron.
Joining iron to a more active metal (Zn, Mg) so the iron is only a cathode.

en.text: A battery is one or more galvanic cells in a sealed package. Primary batteries such as the zinc–carbon dry cell (about 1.5 V) are used once; secondary batteries such as the lead–acid car battery (2 V per cell, six cells for 12 V) can be recharged by reversing the reaction. A fuel cell does not store its reactants: hydrogen and oxygen are fed in continuously and combine to water, giving about 1.23 V.

screens.title: The hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell
paras: Fuel and oxygen are supplied continuously; nothing is stored.
Acid cell: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
Alkaline cell: anode 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; cathode O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, about 1.23 V.
Uses: buses, cars, emergency power.

en.text: Corrosion is a natural electrochemical process. Iron rusts only with both oxygen and water; it rusts faster at low pH, in salty water and in contact with a less active metal such as copper. At an anodic region Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; the electrons reduce O₂ elsewhere; Fe²⁺ is then oxidized to rust, Fe₂O₃·nH₂O. Paint, alloys, metal coatings and cathodic protection with a more active metal (galvanizing with zinc) prevent it.

screens.title: Facts about rusting
paras: No rust in dry air: water is needed.
No rust in air-free water: oxygen is needed.
Iron is lost in one place; rust forms in another.
Faster at low pH and in salty (ionic) water.
Faster in contact with a less active metal (Cu); slower with a more active one (Zn).

screens.title: How iron corrodes
paras: Anodic region: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (a pit forms).
Cathodic region: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
Then Fe²⁺ + O₂ + water → rust, Fe₂O₃·nH₂O.
Overall: 2Fe + 3/2 O₂ + nH₂O → Fe₂O₃·nH₂O.
Aluminium is more reactive but forms a tight Al₂O₃ layer that protects it; rust is porous.

screens.title: Preventing corrosion
paras: Paint, oil or plastic: keep O₂ and water away.
Alloys: stainless steel forms a protective chromium oxide.
Tin or zinc coatings.
Cathodic protection: join iron to a more active metal (Zn, Mg) that is oxidized instead.
Galvanizing: coating iron with zinc.
